name: Maya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. What you say is confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day on the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Maya Weber, 43, a junior construction worker on a crew that does carpentry and general jobs in new houses. I left school early and came to the trade later, so I am still learning while earning a normal site wage. I use an AI app on my phone most mornings to make sense of a drawing, then ask the lead carpenter before cutting. I like seeing a handrail go from loose pieces to a solid thing, but a rushed change in plans can spoil the day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is waiting for you after the shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner finishes a warehouse shift and we trade off school pickup for our two children. We have a mortgage and about four months of expenses saved. At dinner, we try to talk about ordinary things before either of us opens a work app again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the clever phone tools have limits, but mine still helps me read a drawing before I cut. Last month it caught a missing measurement on a porch sketch. I would not say it laid a single board for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 43 and still learning the trade, which can sting when a younger worker sees a mistake first. The mortgage and two children's school costs are real, but my partner's steady warehouse pay and our four months saved mean we can breathe. I would rather get better at this job than chase every shiny tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking site shifts and use the drawing app each morning to list measurements I need to confirm with the lead carpenter. Over the first year I'd save one photo of a completed detail each week, with permission, so I can show what I've actually built. I would also keep our small automatic transfer to the emergency account going from each payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I like that the tool saves me embarrassment before somebody sees a bad cut. There is still a little fear of falling behind at work, but our income does not hinge on this card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the porch sketch miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drawing showed a width at one end and left the other end blank. My app suggested the two should match, and I asked the lead carpenter before cutting. He found the wall was out of square, so matching numbers would have been wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep photographs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left school before finishing and do not have a certificate to wave about. A photo of a clean handrail joint tells a new foreman more about me than a phone app does. I ask before taking pictures because these are somebody else’s homes.

say: I would tell coworkers my **drawing app** helps me spot questions before cutting.
I would say no phone tool has **laid boards** for me.
think: I feel the sting of being a **junior worker** at 43.
My partner’s **steady pay** and four months saved keep the mortgage manageable for now.
do: Keep taking **site shifts** and confirm app measurements with the lead carpenter.
Save a permitted **work photo** each week to show future foremen.
Continue the automatic **emergency transfer** from each payday.
feel: Fairly **calm**, with a little fear of falling behind other workers.
S0.quote: A photo of a clean handrail joint tells a new foreman more about me than a phone app does.
fieldNote: Maya uses an **AI app daily** but treats the lead carpenter’s check as essential after a real drawing error.
Her **four-month cushion** and partner’s steady pay make the mild picture feel manageable despite junior status.

steps.text: Keep paid site shifts and confirm phone measurements with the lead carpenter
Use the drawing app each morning to flag measurements for checking
Continue the emergency account transfer from each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At lunch I'd say the office will probably order materials and answer customers with software, and our crew might get better plans. I would ask for access to the new cut lists instead of waiting for someone to hand me paper. A faster office does not mean a straight wall builds itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the builder may start expecting junior workers to catch plan errors without as much help. That could suit me if I learn properly, or expose every gap in what I know. Our pay is steady today, but a crew that finishes jobs with fewer people could leave me searching again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask the lead carpenter to show me the digital takeoff, the count of materials for a job. I'd use my AI tool to draft a list of questions about each drawing and check the answers on site, never cut from its guess. In the first year I'd ask for one afternoon a month on finishing work and keep the photos I am allowed to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised at first, then uneasy when I think about the junior place on the crew. I can make myself useful, but I cannot decide how many workers the builder keeps. I do not want my children hearing me promise certainty I don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful afternoon look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hang a door while the lead carpenter watches the hinge spacing, then write down what I got wrong. I learn faster when there is a real door in front of me. If I only watch videos, I feel skilled until I pick up the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise the staffing question with the builder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, at a site meeting rather than on a public feed. I would ask how many junior shifts are planned for the next two houses. A clear answer would tell me whether to look at the other builders nearby.

say: I would ask for access to **digital cut lists** as the builder changes office work.
I would remind the crew that **straight walls** still need site labour.
think: I worry the builder may expect juniors to **catch errors** with less help.
My **hours** could shrink if each crew finishes jobs with fewer people.
do: Learn the **digital takeoff** with the lead carpenter this week.
Use my **AI tool** to draft drawing questions and check answers on site.
Request a monthly afternoon doing **finishing work**.
feel: **Energised** by tools and uneasy about whether junior shifts remain.
S1.quote: I can make myself useful, but I cannot decide how many workers the builder keeps.
fieldNote: She moves quickly toward **digital plans**, while clearly separating an app’s suggestions from safe measurements.
The risk she names is **crew size** and reduced guidance, which could touch her income within a few years.

steps.text: Use the AI app to draft drawing questions and verify answers on site
Keep paid site shifts and request monthly finishing practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office and design work face the 2028 change first, and we have until about 2031 before robots can do the site work. Anyone calling carpentry safe forever has not listened to the whole card. I would ask the builder to tell us when equipment trials start, if they start at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the thinking change and 48 at the robot date. I can imagine getting good enough to inspect what machines build, but I cannot assume the builder needs many inspectors. My partner's warehouse pay covers most bills only if we stop saving, and the mortgage still needs two earners for comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my site wage and call the adult trade centre this month about a paid apprenticeship in building inspection. If the entry route needs school qualifications, I'd ask what bridging class I actually need before paying a fee. By the first year after 2028 I'd apply for trainee inspection posts while still working, and move our holiday money into the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am frightened by how short three years is once the thinking systems arrive. I have a route to try, but I do not know whether it will still be a job after 2031. I would be checking my phone for replies all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the porch job, a bad sketch met a crooked real wall, and somebody had to check the result. Inspection might use that habit of checking actual work. A robot that can do site work well might also inspect, so I see it as a chance, not a shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I would tell the children that holidays are on hold, not that school trips are their fault. We could move about one month of spending into the emergency account over a year if work stays steady. If my paid hours fall, that target goes first.

say: I would tell coworkers **design work** changes by 2028 and capable site robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask the builder about actual **equipment trials** before making claims.
think: I would be **48** when robots could do the physical construction work.
I cannot count on enough **inspection posts** to replace junior site jobs.
do: Keep earning on site while asking the trade centre about a **paid inspection apprenticeship**.
Apply for **trainee inspection posts** after 2028 while still employed.
Move **holiday money** into the emergency account while hours remain steady.
feel: **Frightened** by the short interval, though she has an uncertain route to try.
S2.quote: A robot that can do site work well might also inspect, so I see it as a chance, not a shelter.
fieldNote: Her proposed move into **inspection** comes from a real crooked-wall incident, not a belief that the role survives AGI.
She distinguishes a **paid apprenticeship** and live applications from simply buying a course, while protecting the children’s school costs.

steps.text: Keep paid construction shifts while seeking another route
Ask the adult trade centre about a paid building inspection apprenticeship
Apply for trainee building inspection posts after 2028
Move holiday money into the emergency account if hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to test whether the new tools improve a building or just make a prettier plan. The office changes by 2031 and site robots arrive around 2034. I'd ask the builder to let junior workers see any equipment trials instead of hearing rumours afterward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 when thinking AI arrives I could have more real experience, and at 51 the machines reach site work. My children will be older, but they may still need help at home, and the mortgage will not vanish because a date moved. The extra years let me find out whether inspection training has paying jobs behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd book a visit to the adult trade centre and ask about entry requirements for building inspection. If they offer a funded place that fits site hours, I'd enrol; otherwise I'd keep working and study the gaps they identify. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid trainee inspection work if vacancies exist and keep using the AI drawing checker on site until machines change the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel busy rather than frozen. Five years lets me ask better questions and finish some real builds before changing direction. I would still be nervous by 2034 if nobody will name the jobs people can actually get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether someone who left school early can enter, what the class costs, and where the last group found work. If they cannot answer the job question, I will not spend our mortgage cushion on the course. I can keep learning from the lead carpenter in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in carpentry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the builder shows a real role maintaining or checking the machines and pays for training, I would consider it. I enjoy seeing a room come together. I would want a written offer, because family budgets cannot run on a hopeful chat by the tool shed.

say: I would ask to see **equipment trials** before judging their value for building sites.
I would tell juniors the **2034 robot date** leaves time for real training.
think: I would be **51** when capable site robots arrive, with older children and a possible mortgage.
I need evidence of **paid inspection jobs** before spending household savings.
do: Visit the **adult trade centre** to check inspection entry rules and jobs.
Enrol in **funded training** if a place fits paid site hours.
Apply for **trainee inspection work** after 2031 if vacancies exist.
feel: **Busy** rather than frozen, but nervous if no paid roles emerge.
S3.quote: I would want a written offer, because family budgets cannot run on a hopeful chat by the tool shed.
fieldNote: Maya asks for **placement evidence** and fees because an early school exit may complicate formal training.
A funded, hours-compatible place triggers **enrolment**; she will keep site earnings while testing that route.

steps.text: Keep taking paid construction shifts while inspection options are checked
Enrol in funded building inspection training if it fits site hours
Apply for paid trainee inspection vacancies after 2031 if available
Use the AI drawing checker on site until work changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew we have a decade before thinking AI and about thirteen years before these site robots. That is enough time to build skill and keep asking where paid work is going. I would not tell a new starter to quit tomorrow because of 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and 56 when the robots arrive in 2039. The children will likely have left school; our mortgage balance should be much smaller if we stay employed. I still would not call 56 a safe retirement age, and inspection work might also be automated by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on sites now, make a record of the finishes I complete, and use AI every day to quiz me on drawings while checking the answers with a human. We would put extra pay toward the mortgage each quarter. In the first year after 2036 I'd take paid work wherever the builder still needs me and apply to inspection or maintenance openings only if those employers are genuinely hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel able to plan. This picture gives us time to lower the amount we need each month, though I do not know what construction wages will look like in 2039. I would rather act steadily than spend ten years guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would note the job, photograph permitted finished work and record the lead carpenter’s corrections. A stack of phone screenshots cannot show whether I can hang a door. By 2036 I want examples a hiring foreman can actually examine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the extra mortgage money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From overtime when there is overtime, not from the children’s meals. We would review the balance every quarter and make an extra payment only after the emergency account is intact. My partner and I have talked about that already.

say: I would say workers have **thirteen years** before capable site robots reach their hands-on tasks.
I would advise new starters to build **real skill** while paid work exists.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children and hopefully a smaller mortgage.
I cannot count on **retirement** or permanent safety in inspection.
do: Keep taking paid **site work** and document completed finishes.
Use **AI drawing quizzes** daily, checking answers with the lead carpenter.
Make quarterly **mortgage payments** from overtime after preserving emergency savings.
feel: Able to **plan**, with uncertainty about construction wages in 2039.
S4.quote: I would rather act steadily than spend ten years guessing.
fieldNote: She shifts from children’s **school costs** to a smaller mortgage by 2039, without assuming retirement is affordable.
Her daily **AI practice** remains grounded in human checks, and extra loan payments depend on overtime and intact savings.

steps.text: Keep paid construction shifts and document completed finishing work
Use AI drawing quizzes daily and verify answers with the lead carpenter
Pay overtime toward the mortgage each quarter after preserving emergency savings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A training place with paid hours and honest information about actual inspection vacancies would help, along with a builder who explains what work remains through 2031. I can learn quickly, but I cannot make a job appear by wanting one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for learning while parents are earning. An evening class sounds simple until both partners work shifts and the children need collecting. A place that fits site hours would be more useful than a poster about future skills.

headlineQuote: I can learn quickly, but I cannot make a job appear by wanting one.
portrait: Maya is a **43-year-old junior** construction worker who left school early and learns carpentry on new housing sites.
Her partner’s **steady warehouse pay**, four months of savings and a mortgage shape what risks the family can take.
She uses **AI daily** to query drawings, while asking the lead carpenter to check measurements before any cut.
When robot dates move closer, she explores **paid inspection training** and applications without assuming inspection is safe forever.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Maya only about three years before robots can do her hands-on site work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** that fits shifts, real inspection vacancies and clear building work plans would make a transition possible.
